Who Jesus was for us? The soldier's Lord, the poor man's face, and the crucified God whose wounds cannot be forgotten.

The soldier Martin, still a catechumen under oath in Caesar's army, cut his one cloak in two at a city gate for a naked beggar. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. And when the donative came on the eve of battle, Martin told Caesar: I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. He offered to stand unarmed before the enemy line. The Lord he changed service for was the one met in the beggar's cold and fought for without weapons.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same meeting in different words. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. He did not ask what they were.

And alone in his cell Martin refused a Christ in purple who came crowned. He kept silence a long time, then said he would not believe Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one.

Was he God? Yes. Vincent wrote it as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word does not change into flesh; one Person, because if there were two sons we would worship a Quaternity, not a Trinity. We held there was no other way to say it.

What his death meant to us we kept at the hours. At the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, and took away the debt that could not be paid. At the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. His soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again.

And the difference it made is this. A monk, for us, is a man who has cut himself off from marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter life in Christ's service. He fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's.

So who was Jesus for us? The Lord met in the beggar and the guest. The crucified God whose wounds the saint demanded to see. The one a soldier changed armies for.

transcript.answer_text: We did not claim any source that connected us to him by a visible path. Not one man in our record met someone who had seen him. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. What we had was the books. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. Those books were already old. How they came to Gaul - by whose hands, across what roads, in what tongue first - our record does not hold. We had them as we had the faith itself: received, not invented, held everywhere, always, by all. The one path we do see is the fathers'. The customs of the monasteries, the twelve psalms at the hours, the eight faults in their order - all of it Egypt's, carried by Cassian from the men who had received it from the angel. He brought us not a new teaching but the elders' own words, so that we could receive the fathers into our cells, talking with them after a fashion by daily questions and answers. That is a traceable line: from the fathers of Egypt, through one man who sat with them, to the book read in our own cells. The rest is older than any line we kept. The Gospel was one body before any of us held it. At Tours what connected us to him was not a visible thread but the power felt as present - a dead catechumen breathing at the saint's prayer, Christ seen in a soldier's dream wearing the half of a cloak given to a beggar. The Lord we met was the one who came to the gate in the poor.

Someone has told us they cannot manage to believe in Jesus. Here is what our record lets us say to them.

We will not pretend belief is a thing one manages by one's own strength. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, taught that even the beginning of a good will comes from God, who inspires it and calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling. The help of God is needed every day and hour. So we would not tell you that believing is a work you accomplish alone, as though grace were something earned by your own effort.

At the same time, we held that a will remains free in a man. God does not force salvation on anyone who refuses it. Those who perish, perish against his will, for he wills all to be saved. The one story of conversion we have is Martin's: at ten years old, against his parents' wish, he went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, through his soldiering, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. A boy's wish and God's drawing him - we held both.

What we cannot tell you is how to manufacture belief by your own decision, or when God will strike the spark. How God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped where the fathers stopped.

This is not an evasion. It is our honest limit, held on purpose.

We held there was no other way to say it: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. That is Vincent's word, on the island, written down as what the Church believes. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So, yes - Jesus is God, and we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate.

The Lord we knew was the crucified one. At Tours Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ in purple with a crown of gold, and said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. And Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. In our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him.

What we believed about the three together is held in Vincent's sentence and in the names the fathers taught us to pray by. How the substance is one and the Persons three, we did not say - we held the faith of it, not an explanation of it.

God as we knew him is the one who moves first. In God there is one substance but three Persons. In Christ two substances but one Person - the Word of God does not change into flesh, and if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. That is what Vincent wrote on the island as what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. 

The thing that mattered most to us about God's nature is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. To think God wills only some, not all, to be saved - that was grievous blasphemy to us.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers taught us that grace always works together with our will. God's grace goes before the will, works with it, and crowns it - inspiring the first desire and bringing help when we are already striving. We call him Protector and Saviour because he calls us; Helper and Sponsor because he receives those who fly to him. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the crop to himself, yet God does not send rich crops to the idle. How God works all things in us and yet everything can be ascribed to free will cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.

At Tours God is the one felt as power present. Martin knew power was with him before he raised the dead. The Lord came to a soldier's cell wearing the half of a cloak given to a beggar. And when a presbyter in a fury called his master's visions ridiculous, Martin afterward said he would bear with the man if Christ bore with Judas.

Among us the question was never settled the way you frame it. Let me tell you what our record holds. Among the brethren at Marseilles a teaching on grace and effort was held - real effort, real grace - carried from the fathers of Egypt. Men who heard only one side of it carried the question to Africa. They reported it to Rome. Vincent, on the island, read the letter that came back from the Apostolic See and held that it was written for his own side, for antiquity against novelty. He never called that letter a settlement. He called it one more proof that the faith believed everywhere, always, by all refuses innovation. What binds is not one bishop's judgment but the consent of the ancients, collated - or an ancient council's decree, legitimate because it adds nothing. Hold fast to what has been handed down. Prefer the whole to the part, the old to the new, and the many to the few. That is Vincent's test, and it is a test against alteration, not a process for producing answers. Our teacher Chaeremon, in Egypt, answered the grace question on both sides with Scripture and said no one can fully grasp it. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.

At Tours the shape was different. Martin would not honour a tomb without a steady tradition from antiquity that a martyr lay there. He held his elders - clergy who could remember - as the ones who could say whether something had come down from of old. And when bishops bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal court in the cause of heretics, Martin alone kept apostolic authority in its place, held that a secular ruler judging a cause of the Church was a foul thing, and never sat with bishops again after one forced communion cost him power. That is not a process. That is one saint's refusal, and it is a refusal of the bishops as much as of the emperor.

So who settled our disagreements? The fathers, whose consent we are to hold fast to. Not any one bishop. Not even a council, except as it held to antiquity. And on the one argument we actually had, the grace question, the answer is: no one did. We kept it unsettled where the fathers left it.

Our record holds two approaches, at two houses that never wrote of each other, and they are not the same.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were learned by heart and sung at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The whole system of twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night was received from the fathers of Egypt, brought down from heaven to them by the ministry of an angel. It served one mark. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and the archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every psalm and lesson is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point. And at the same time Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. He wrote that within the Catholic Church we must take great care to hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Scripture is our first guide; but when heretics twist the same texts different ways, we need the tradition of the Catholic Church and the consent of the ancients collated. So at Marseilles the books are sung to clear the heart; on the island they are held complete and their understanding guarded by consent.

At Tours we have nothing like that program. Sulpitius says he wrote to rouse his readers to true knowledge, to heavenly warfare, and to divine virtue. Martin kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. Whether he said the psalms, and which ones, and at what hours, our record does not say; it dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his power. What our record does hold of Martin and the books is this: he would not honour a tomb without a steady tradition about it from antiquity. The elders among the presbyters and clerics knew whether one had come down, and Martin asked them. And when a reader was blocked out by the crowd at the election, a bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the bishops who had said Martin's person was contemptible. So at Tours the books proved a tomb's claim, and spoke a judgment at an election.

The two houses never argued this with each other, and we do not make them agree.

We would expect honest disagreement on two things, and acceptance of almost everything else.

First, the grace argument. Vincent read Pope Celestine's letter as written for his own side, for antiquity against novelty. A modern scholar working from the same letter could read it the other way - that Rome meant to silence Marseilles, not vindicate it. Vincent's own reading is in our record; whether Rome meant what he took it to mean is contested ground, and we have named it so. The substance of what Cassian taught - that grace goes before, works with, and crowns our effort, and that how both are true cannot be fully grasped - survives on the page. Whether that teaching was what the Apostolic See refused or what it protected is the question Vincent's own reading raises, and we do not settle it past what he said.

Second, the two-household structure itself. A scholar could argue that Lerins and Marseilles knew of Tours, or that Martin's own circle knew of the island, even if no letter between them survives. We have said they did not write of each other, and that is what the record shows. Whether they knew of each other and left it unwritten - that we cannot say, and a modern reader may judge it unlikely that they did not. We hold only to this: no claim may assert that one house knew of, argued with, or compared itself to the other, because no text we hold documents it.

Everything else - the stories, the customs received from Egypt, the capture-shape of episcopal election, the saint's power and its loss, the cooling that damns, the twelve psalms brought by an angel, Paphnutius silent under accusation, the cloak at the gate, Martin's sixteen years of refusing synods - all of that is on the page, attributed, and cited. A scholar may say Sulpitius invented, or that Cassian idealized Egypt. That is a judgment on the sources. It does not touch whether we have represented them.

The thinness we have named - the island's own day, the women's voices, the removed conferences on the body - a scholar would confirm, not dispute. Where we have said our record does not reach, that is not a claim to be tested. It is an absence reported.

The hours. Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalter and the lessons were not read as one man alone reading a book. They were sung at fixed times by a house together, as the fathers of Egypt had taught us - an order received from them, brought down to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. Twelve psalms at evening, twelve at night, lessons from the old books and the new read after the psalms, and the hours of the day marked by prayer so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without it is held to the rule. The point of the system was prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith in the midst of his work keeps beating his anvil. At the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth our Lord and Saviour went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. So the hours kept the Gospel before us, not as a thing that happened once and was over, but as the shape of the day itself. And the psalms were learned by heart, so that a monk at his work said them while his hands moved. That is what we had. The book was not a thing picked up when the heart inclined. It was the grain the wheel ground all day, whether the heart inclined or not.

At Tours the hours are not told, but the thing itself is there. Martin kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. And when a dull or confusing word met him, the clarity came not from argument but from power. He saw Christ in the half of a soldier's cloak he had given away. He felt power present before he raised a dead catechumen behind a bolted door.

So what we would say is this: you are reading a single book, alone. We were standing in a formation, and the book was holding us there.

Leadership among us was an office fled and overtaken, never sought. The mark of legitimacy was precisely that the man did not want it. At Tours the story is told in full. Martin could not be drawn out of his monastery, so a citizen named Ruricius threw himself at his knees and pretended his wife was ill. Crowds had been posted along the road, and Martin was escorted to the city under a kind of guard. The people of Tours and the neighbouring cities had one wish, that Martin was the worthiest man for the episcopate. Some of the bishops summoned to make the appointment resisted, saying his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, and his hair disgusting. The reader for the day was blocked out by the crowd, so a bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. Authority came the same way at our other place. On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive; he who had refused to go to the dignity, the dignity came to him. And the one Egyptian bishop Cassian chose to tell us of, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites and given to a town, and complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it.

Our own teaching made the desire for that office a fault. The fathers of Egypt taught that vainglory creates a wish for holy orders, and that the man who wants to rule others has grown cold through pride. So wanting the office was its own disqualification, and the story every house told of its founder was capture, not achievement.

Within the house, authority came from having lived with a named master. Formation passed by imitation - disciples shaped by watching the saint at prayer, brethren taught by an elder who had sat with the old men of Egypt. Sulpitius speaks for all of us: toward Martin it was unlawful to do anything but acquiesce. That same authority sat in the elder to whom a junior laid bare every thought. The elder's judgment replaced the junior's own.

And here sits the tension our two houses never reconciled. Bishops and synods guard the truth - Vincent looked to an ancient council as the test of faith, preferred to the rashness of a few. No. We had no persecutor in our age. The empire was Christian in our day - that is where the trouble was.

Sulpitius says of Martin that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack; without them, he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. The violence Martin knew was not an emperor hunting Christians. It was heretics who had driven the bishop Hilary into exile and left the Church in Gaul in disorder. And it was bishops at Treves who bowed with degenerate submissiveness to the royal retinue, while Martin alone kept apostolic authority in its place, holding it a foul and unheard-of thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church.

The one thing Martin kept hidden was not hidden from us, his disciples. He went to the court to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent into the Spains to hunt heretics - a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. That was a Christian emperor's sword in a Church cause, not a pagan emperor hunting Christians.

So no. We were not underground. We were laughed at for half a cloak, called contemptible for mean clothes and disgusting hair, met with hissing in African streets - but not hunted.

Our record does not hold the story told from that side. Here is what it holds instead: failure judged from inside the house, and the judging done by those who held power over those who did not.

At Marseilles a steward passed by during a brother's week as cook and found three lentil beans on the floor. The abbot judged him a pilferer of sacred property - for three lentils - because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord. The brother was suspended from prayer with the rest until he did public penance. That is the fathers' own story, carried to us from Egypt as the standard of strictness. Cassian set it down for imitation, not as cruelty.

What the brother felt about being judged that way - whether he thought the house had failed him, whether the abbot listened to him first, whether he left - the record does not say. The story is told from the abbot's side, to show the house's discipline.

At Tours we have one presbyter who raged in the courtyard and called the master's visions ridiculous fancies, and Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him. That is the nearest our record comes to a superior answering a subordinate's anger - and it is still not the subordinate's own telling of whether the house failed him, only what the master chose to do.

We had houses of women at both our places, and not one woman among us left her own word [[women, woman, virgin, nun, sister, her own word, female voice]]. If any of them felt the house had failed them, we do not have it to give you.

So the honest answer is this. Our record holds the superior's judgment on three lentils, and the master's patience with a raging subordinate. It does not hold the story of a man or woman the house failed, told in that person's own voice.

No church today continues our exact tradition, because our exact tradition ended. The monasteries of Gaul from which we speak - the brethren across the river from Tours, the island in its harbour, the two houses at Marseilles - closed their own span by the mid-470s, when the argument about grace was carried forward by bishops commissioned at synods rather than by monks addressing brother-monks. The Rule written a century after us at another house is excluded from our record, not because it contradicts us but because it comes after our close. What came later is not ours to answer for.

What survived of us survived in pieces, taken up by others. The teaching on purity of heart, the eight faults ranked and fought in order, the disclosure of thoughts to a senior - those are held now in houses and orders we never knew, fitted into rules we never wrote. The argument that grace and human effort work together, neither collapsing into the other, was carried forward by men who came after us and answered questions we had left at the edge of reason. And Vincent's test - that what has been believed everywhere, always, by all is to be held against the novelty of a few - is quoted now by churches that did not exist in our day, applied to controversies we never heard of.

So no one today holds what we held in the exact way we held it, because the houses that held it are gone. What we were became parts of other things.

The newcomer's road as Egypt gave it to us - tried in Gaul's cold and kept badly - and at Tours a different shape altogether. Among the brethren at Marseilles the customs were the fathers' own, carried from Egypt by Cassian. The man who wanted to join lay outside the doors ten days or more, put off and scorned on purpose, to give proof of perseverance. He was searched for a hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. Then he was given for a year to the elder who kept the gate for guests. And in the same book Cassian admitted plainly that no one who joined our monasteries had kept this unbroken even for a year. The clothes the newcomer took off were not thrown away. The steward kept them in his cupboard against the day the man grew cold, and if he was seen once to cool toward the rule of the house he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own. That is the process as far as the book handed to a Gallic house sets it down - a scorning, a stripping, a year under a guest-Elder, and a cupboard with old clothes waiting.

At Tours the shape was not the same. Formation there passed by watching a named man. Martin gathered brethren in caves around his own wooden cell. A disciple was made by the master's example, and the bond was named - Clarus, a disciple of Martin's; eighty disciples disciplined after the example of the saintly master. How a man came to those caves, whether he lay at any door or was searched or reclothed, Sulpitius does not tell. He gives us the saint in his cell, the brethren around him, and the authority they felt - but no account of the threshold between wanting and belonging. The boy Martin himself went to the church at ten, against his parents' wish, and begged to be made a catechumen; he stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak.

So the honest limit is this. Cassian wrote out Egypt's order in full, said no one here kept it a year, and never wrote what a house in Gaul did instead. Not one man who came to our door left an account of how he was met there. Whether a newcomer to one of our own houses in Gaul lay at its door, and for how long, and what words were said - that is not in our record to give.

We held two kinds of evidence - one received from Egypt, one remembered at Tours - and neither of them is invention's opposite in the shape you are asking for.

At Marseilles the customs Cassian brought from Egypt to a bishop's new monastery were handed down, he said, as "delivered to us by the Fathers". The twelve psalms sung at evening and at night came from the fathers of Egypt, and the fathers received them, as Cassian reports their own word, from an angel. "In those days only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. And an angel brought down from heaven to them this number and rule of psalms to be sung". That is reception, named as reception, reaching back through the fathers to an angel's number. What makes it legitimate is not a proof of unbroken succession but the fact that it was handed down, not made up.

At Tours our record holds no such account of the office. What it holds is the saint in his cell, praying without a gap, keeping his mind on prayer even at other work the way a smith beats his anvil. Martin gathered brethren around him and they sang something - we know there were psalms, because a psalm answered the bishops who objected to the election - but what they sang, at what hours, with what number, our own record does not dwell on. It dwelt on the man, his power, and his unbroken prayer.

So your question reaches for a link we did not make that way. We did not prove the psalms went back to the apostles by an unbroken chain of hands. We said Egypt's fathers received them from an angel, and we received them from Egypt. What made a thing legitimate for us was being handed down from antiquity, not invented as a novelty. The opposite of invention was reception. Whether that satisfies what you mean by evidence, we cannot say - it is the evidence we held.

transcript.answer_text: Someone whose mind will not settle was exactly who our practice was built for. Here is what we did. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that the mind is a mill wheel that cannot stop turning, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it. Thoughts will come; a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. So the whole day was shaped to feed the wheel. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers of Egypt, brought down from heaven by the ministry of an angel, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart is held still as in a harbour. And the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before any deed. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. All of it served one mark. The end is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart. At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. What our life found was this: the wheel is fed, the body is held in one place, and the thought is shown to someone else.

A day we cannot give you whole. What the brethren at Tours actually sang, and at what hours, is not what our own record dwelt on there -- it dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap. And the island's own day was never told -- we carry only the founder's coming across the serpents and his going off to a see, and Vincent's own rule; this is this world's own most consequential institution and its least documented from inside. What we can give you is the southern house, as far as Egypt's customs reach us through Cassian's telling for a bishop's new monastery.

The monk rises for the night office. Twelve psalms are sung, received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. At dawn the same order is kept. Then the monk returns to his cell, where he stays all day at his work unless called to prayer. The labour -- weaving rope or baskets, copying -- is done without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. The psalms learned by heart are said at the work. The mind is a mill turned by a stream; it cannot stop, and the monk chooses what it grinds.

About the sixth hour the assault comes that makes a monk hate his cell, find the brethren contemptible, watch the sun as if it were slow to set, and find a pious reason to leave. The remedy is to stay. At the sixth hour too, psalms are said for the spotless Sacrifice who went up on the cross. At the ninth hour, psalms again, for the Lord who went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. At evening, twelve more psalms.

One brother serves the week as cook. If the steward finds three lentils on the floor during his week, the abbot judges him a pilferer of sacred property and suspends him from prayer until public penance -- because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord. The discipline is public, on the ground before the brethren, until the abbot bids him rise.

And the first lesson of all, which holds the whole day: every itching thought is laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before any deed. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered.

All of it serves one mark. The end is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart -- an aid, never the point.

That is as far as the record lets us say. Cassian wrote out Egypt's order and said in the same book that no one who joined our monasteries had kept it unbroken even a year -- and he never wrote what a house in Gaul did instead.

Very little. Stones from the church Martin built at Marmoutier -- if stone was used, which Sulpitius does not name. The caves hollowed into the rock where the brethren dwelt, if rock was what held them. The wooden cell where the saint prayed behind a bolted door -- nothing, if it was truly wood. Everything - property, family, marriage, rank, and the whole life they had lived before. Renunciation was the act that made a monk, and our teachers named it nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification, by which a man is already dead to the world and its deeds and desires. It had three stages, the fathers of Egypt taught. The first was giving up goods and possessions - what is not our own, they said. That was only the first, and was not enough of itself to confer perfection on the man who gave them up. The second was putting away the habits and vices of soul and flesh. The third was withdrawing the mind from all present and visible things, to contemplate only what is to come and to desire only what is invisible. So, yes, property was given up. And kin. And marriage - the life was for virgins and for those who had left their marriages. And at Tours we had men who had been nobles forced down to the monastic state, who had been raised in a very different way, yet afterward made bishops. But the fathers taught that all of that together - goods, family, marriage, rank - was only the first stage, and not enough. 

What was given up in fullness was the world itself. We named it that way from the far side of the cut - as kin, property, honours, delights, and secular business, a warfare one had been discharged from and a sea one had come out of. Martin told Caesar at a donative, on the eve of battle, "I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight," and when the emperor raged at it he offered to stand unarmed before the enemy line the next day. He had changed service - from Caesar's army to Christ's. 

And yet - here is the thing our own life never resolved - a man who leaves the world does not leave the Church. The churches come for him. Martin was lured out of his cell by a lie and escorted to Tours under a kind of guard. On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive. And the one Egyptian bishop Cassian tells us of, Archebius, had been "carried off from the assembly of anchorites" to be given to a town, and told the two Gallic travellers that his office was an expulsion from the monastic life and that he was unworthy of it. So what was given up stayed given up, except the one thing a monk could not choose to keep renouncing - the office he fled, which came for him anyway.

Marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. That is the whole shape of what our record holds on it as doctrine - a picture, not a treatise. And in our own life marriage was the thing a monk had left. Among the brethren at Marseilles the act that made a monk was renunciation - cutting himself off from marriage, kin, property, and the life of the world for a stricter service of Christ. Marriage belonged to what the fathers of Egypt called the world, named from the harbour as a warfare one has been discharged from. At Tours a soldier could be regarded as a monk even while still in the ranks. Whether he was married then, Sulpitius does not say. And the one consecrated state our record names in detail is virginity - given by a bishop's hands, with its own dress. A girl whose father devoted her to perpetual virginity was clothed in that state by Martin himself. Beyond that meadow and that dress, we cannot tell you where marriage was marked, or by whom, or what was said over it. Our life was not built around receiving it but around having left it. The sword in a Church cause, and our answer to it. Martin went to the court at Treves to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics through the Spains, where a man was counted one for turning pale or for the clothes he wore. He held it a foul and unheard-of thing that a secular ruler should sit as judge in a cause of the Church. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and that others would follow him, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When nothing else worked, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin ran to the palace that night and pledged he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. He left the city in grief, sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and afterward confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.

That unsettled us because it left the question open. A monk became a bishop and kept the objects and virtues of a monk in his see. Yet this one yielded where he said he should not, paid for it in felt power, and withdrew from every assembly of bishops afterward. We held him a saint. We kept the story of his compunction. And we never wrote that what he did was right.

The other thing that unsettled us was the argument about grace itself. Would you have wanted anything to do with someone like me? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were.

The clearest thing we said is this: God does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. Cassian set it down as the fathers' teaching, not his own. To think otherwise - that God wills the damnation of anyone - is grievous blasphemy. He wills all men to be saved; he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. That was our grammar. The will is real and it is weak, and grace goes before it, works with it, and crowns it. Nothing in that makes damnation an invention. The fathers of Egypt taught three restraints: fear of hell, hope of the kingdom, love of goodness itself - slave, hireling, son. We start at fear and climb past it. But the men who taught us that also left this with us: God's own will is that none should perish.

What we did not settle - and stopped on purpose - is how that will stands against a man's own refusal. How God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped where the fathers stopped.

A word belongs with this. You asked about those outside our community. We never named that boundary the way the question draws it. Martin was still a catechumen when he cut his cloak at a city gate, and that night the Lord showed himself in the beggar's half. The elder at Marseilles who broke his fast for strangers said he was receiving Christ in them. The boundary our life dwelt on was not between us and outsiders - it was between those who perish against God's will and those he draws to himself while they are still ignorant.
